Forbidden.description: The credential is known but its role or scope does not cover this operation on this application and environment (`insufficient-scope`), or the call is refused for another reason (`forbidden`). ContestedNodeId.description:
A node id that two live machines are claiming at the same time.

The damage this records is quiet and total. A node id is the whole of a
node's identity here: it keys the fleet list, the health cache, the
delivery fan-out and the cron rotation. When a second machine registers the
id a first machine is still answering for, everything this control plane
sends goes to exactly one of them - and the report for a deployment, or for
an application deletion, counts one node and says every node took it, while
the other machine keeps serving the previous version with the previous
secrets and is never told anything again.

So the claim is refused, the machine already answering keeps the id, and
this record exists to make the machine that was refused visible: every
fan-out names it as unreached, exactly as a [`DepartedNode`] is named.

The probe cannot tell two machines from one machine that has started
reporting a second address while the first still reaches it, and it does
not pretend to: both are answered the same way, because in both the address
that was proven live keeps the id and nothing moves silently. The message
names both readings and the operator action for each.

It is cleared when the refusals stop for a whole registration lifetime -
which is what happens when whichever machine was wrong is corrected or shut
down - or when an operator says the machine is gone with
`DELETE /api/nodes/{id}/registration`.

claimant_addr.description:
The address that was refused the id. Nothing is ever sent here, and
this machine is still running whatever it last had.

first_refused_at.description: First time this claim was refused.

holder_addr.description: The address that holds the id, and the only one anything is sent to.

holder_hostname.description: Hostname of the machine holding the id, when it said one.

last_refused_at.description:
Most recent time it was refused. The claimant keeps registering every
`registration_refresh_interval`, so this is how the record stays alive
and how it expires once the claim stops coming.

ControlListPage_RetiredAppName.description:
The one list envelope of the Control API. Every list route answers in it,
whatever it lists.

items.description:
A name that belonged to an application which has been deleted, and which
is therefore not free.

Deleting an application removes it from this catalog and leaves everything
it stored where it was: deis-store and deis-queue key a tenant by
`(application, environment)` and neither of them has an operation that
drops one. So the name is retained rather than the data, and nothing can
be deployed onto it until somebody says out loud that the next application
of that name may have what the last one left - see
`CatalogStore::release_retired_name`.

environments.description:
The environments it had when it was deleted, in name order.

One environment is one tenant, so this is the list of places its data
still is. It can be empty - an application deleted before it had an
environment - and the name is retained all the same: a storage token
is minted per environment on request, and an environment that was
created and used is not distinguishable here from one that was never
touched.

A name that has been used, deleted, released and used again carries
the environments of every application that had it, because every one
of those tenants may still hold data.

released_at.description:
When an operator freed the name again, if they have.

`None` is a name that is still held, which is the only state that
stops an application being created under it. The row survives the
release rather than being deleted, because what it records - which
tenants hold data under this name - stays true afterwards, and the
next deletion of the same name has to add to that list rather than
start a new one.

retired_at.description: When the application was deleted, Unix epoch seconds.

canonical_artifact_id.description:
Exact provider-neutral parent and provider derivation. Both are absent

oneOf.description:
Which day's platform this version was written against, and which
behaviours that leaves on, resolved from the same stored manifest.

Lifted out of `manifest` deliberately. It is already in there, but the
question "why does this behave differently in production" has to be
answerable without reading a bundle or picking through a manifest, and
this is the field `deis versions` and `deis deploy` print. A version
that declares no date is `Some` with a null date - that is a complete
answer and the one an operator most needs to see.

`None` means the stored manifest could not be read at all, which is the
same condition that leaves `manifest` holding a raw string.

manifest.description: The manifest as structured JSON, parsed from the stored text.

role.description:
One of the names in [`Role`]. Required rather than defaulted: the
difference between `viewer` and `owner` is the whole point, and a
default would be the one somebody forgot to think about.

id.description: App name; also the app_id every component keys off.

name.description:
What this credential is for, in a word: `ci-preview`, `alice-laptop`.
It is printed in every listing, so it is how a person decides which
one to revoke.

scopes.description:
The scope list. Absent means the account's role over every
application (see [`Role::default_scopes`]); an explicit empty list
means a token that can do nothing yet.

unscoped.description:
Ask for a credential subject to no scope at all - the old flat
`api_keys` behaviour. Spelled out rather than implied by an empty
scope list, because "everything" and "nothing" must not be one typo
apart.

retained.description:
What was *not* removed: the name, and the data behind it.

The counters in `removed` are catalog rows. This is the stored data,
which is still in deis-store and deis-queue under the tenants named
here, and the record that keeps the name from being handed to the next
application that asks for it.

retained_note.description:
What the tenants in `retained` mean, in one sentence, for a caller
that is showing this to a person rather than parsing it.

unloaded.description:
Which nodes stopped serving the app, and which did not.

A node in `failed` is still running the deleted application - its
code, its secrets in memory and its queue consumers - so the caller
has to see that here; nothing else will ever mention this app again.

DeletedApp.description:
Everything deleting an app removed. Returned so the caller can clean up
the bundle files on disk and log exactly how much history was destroyed.

DeliveryReason.description:
Why a delivery is happening. Only used for logs and for the answer the
API gives, but it is the difference between "someone deployed" and "a
secret changed under a version that did not move".

DeliveryReport.description:
What came of one delivery. Returned to the API caller so a deploy says
where it actually landed instead of only that a row was written.

delivered.description:
Nodes that acknowledged the requested phase with the exact plan and
generation identity.

failed.description:
Nodes that did not. They keep serving whatever they had until they
refetch their assignments.

phase.description:
Wire phase this report actually observed. This prevents a successful
PREPARE acknowledgement from being presented as though production had
already activated.

skipped.description:
Set when nothing was sent at all, with the reason. A deployment
coordinator must not read this as successful prepare.

DepartedNode.description:
A node this control plane had on its fleet list and then lost.

Losing a registration is not the same as a node going away. It expires
because the node **stopped talking to this control plane**, which is
exactly the state in which it is still running whatever it last received
and cannot be told anything new: it is not reachable for a push, and it is
not asking for its assignments either, so nothing corrects it. Dropping the
entry and remembering nothing is what let a deploy - and, worse, an
application deletion - answer "every node took it" while a live node kept
serving the old code and the deleted app's secrets.

The record is cleared when the node registers again, or when somebody says
the machine is really gone with `DELETE /api/nodes/{id}/registration`.

departed_at.description: When this control plane dropped it from the fleet list.

last_registered_at.description: Last time it refreshed its registration.

version_number.description: Target version by its per-app number, i.e. the "v3" a human says.

Which nodes took this version. Absent when the response only reads

deployment.description:

created under this name is the same storage tenant as the deleted one.

RemovalReport.description:
What came of taking an application off the fleet.

Deleting an application is the one operation whose failure is silent
without this: the rows are gone from the catalog, so nothing will ever
mention the app again, while a node that was not reached keeps serving
it - with its code, its secrets in memory and its queue consumers still
polling - until that process restarts.

environments.description:
Environment names the catalog had for this app when it was deleted.
Informational: the nodes are told to drop every environment of it.

failed.description: Nodes that did not. **These still serve the deleted application.**

skipped.description: Set when nothing was sent at all, with the reason.

unloaded.description: Nodes that dropped it and no longer serve it.

RetiredAppName.description:
A name that belonged to an application which has been deleted, and which
is therefore not free.

Deleting an application removes it from this catalog and leaves everything
it stored where it was: deis-store and deis-queue key a tenant by
`(application, environment)` and neither of them has an operation that
drops one. So the name is retained rather than the data, and nothing can
be deployed onto it until somebody says out loud that the next application
of that name may have what the last one left - see
`CatalogStore::release_retired_name`.

environments.description:
The environments it had when it was deleted, in name order.

One environment is one tenant, so this is the list of places its data
still is. It can be empty - an application deleted before it had an
environment - and the name is retained all the same: a storage token
is minted per environment on request, and an environment that was
created and used is not distinguishable here from one that was never
touched.

A name that has been used, deleted, released and used again carries
the environments of every application that had it, because every one
of those tenants may still hold data.

released_at.description:
When an operator freed the name again, if they have.

`None` is a name that is still held, which is the only state that
stops an application being created under it. The row survives the
release rather than being deleted, because what it records - which
tenants hold data under this name - stays true afterwards, and the
next deletion of the same name has to add to that list rather than
start a new one.

retired_at.description: When the application was deleted, Unix epoch seconds.

Role.description:
What an account is allowed to hold.

A role is a ceiling, not a grant: it says which verbs this account's
tokens may carry, and it is re-checked on every request rather than only
when a token is minted. That is what makes a demotion mean something -
moving an account from `owner` to `viewer` reduces every token it already
holds to reading, at the next request, without anybody having to hunt
those tokens down.

must send back in `x-deis-tenant` on every storage call. Included so
a caller never has to rebuild it, and so the one this control plane
signed is visible to anyone debugging a refused call.

answer predates it and is kept byte for byte on every prefix.

question "why does this behave differently in production" has to be
answerable without reading a bundle or picking through a manifest, and
this is the field `deis versions` and `deis deploy` print. A version
that declares no date is `Some` with a null date - that is a complete
answer and the one an operator most needs to see.

`None` means the stored manifest could not be read at all, which is the

info.description: The human API of the Deislet control plane: the product API under `/api/v1` and the platform diagnostics under `/api/platform`. Every paginated collection answers in the `ControlListPage` envelope with an opaque cursor; four platform diagnostics still answer a shape of their own and take no cursor (`listAllRoutes`, `listSessions`, `listNodeConfigs`, `listRuntimeFleet`). nodes that were on the list, stopped refreshing their registration and are
presumed to be still running what they last received. Every deploy and
every application deletion names them as unreached, so an operator has to
be able to see which ones they are and clear the ones whose machine is
really gone with `DELETE /api/nodes/{id}/registration`.

`contested` is the third: machines that registered a node id another
machine was already answering for and were refused it. They are running
this platform's code, nothing can be sent to them, and they are on no other
list - so this is where an operator finds out that two machines were given

This is a node-local operation and changes nothing in the catalog, which
is why it is **refused** while the catalog still deploys the application:
a node reconciles against `GET /api/nodes/{id}/assignments` on its own
timer, that list is built from the catalog and names the same application,
and the node loads it straight back. The endpoint used to send the unload
anyway and answer `200 {"success": true}`, so an operator was told the
application was off a node while the node was already putting it back -
and there was nothing in the answer, or anywhere else, to say so. An
operation that reports success and then reverses itself is worse than one
that refuses, because the refusal is the only version of it an operator
can act on.

What it is still for: an application the catalog no longer names but a node
is still running - a node that was unreachable when the application was
deleted, or one that has drifted. That case is the one where the unload
sticks, because the next assignment list will not contain it either.

delete.description:
Removes the app together with its versions, environments, deployment
history, routes and secrets, drops the bundle files those versions
referenced, and tells every node to stop serving it.

That last step is not optional. A node adds applications from its
assignment list and never removes one that has left it, so a delete that
only touched the database would leave every node serving the application
forever: still answering requests, still holding its decrypted secrets
in memory, still polling its queues. A delete done to revoke access has
to actually revoke it, so a node that cannot be reached is reported in
the answer rather than passed over.

What it does *not* remove is the application's stored data. That lives in
deis-store and deis-queue, keyed by `(application, environment)`, and this
control plane has no call that drops a tenant there, so the answer reports
the tenants that still hold it and the name is retained so that the next
application of that name cannot be handed it silently.

The names of deleted applications and the tenants whose data is the reason
they are held. This is the only record of what became of a deleted
application's data: its catalog rows are gone, and deis-store and
deis-queue cannot be asked what they still hold.

A row with `released_at` set is a name somebody freed again: it can be
created, and what it says about the data is as true as it ever was.

delete.description:
Free the name again. Deliberately a second call, made by an administrator,
rather than something the delete could have done on its own: releasing it
is the decision that the next application created under this name may have
whatever the deleted one left in deis-store and deis-queue. Whoever makes
it is in the audit log, and so is this call when it is refused.

The data itself is untouched either way. An operator who wants it gone
purges it - `deis kv`, `deis db`, `deis blob` against those tenants while
the application still exists, or the tenant's files under deis-store's own
data directory - and then releases the name.
